arXiv:2002.10995v2 [math.AG] 31 Jul 2021

Classification of smooth factorial affine surfaces
of Kodaira dimension zero with trivial units

Tomasz Pełka Address: Basque Center for Applied Mathematics, Alameda de Mazarredo 14, 48009 Bilbao, Spain Email address: tpelka@bcamath.org and Paweł Raźny Address: Instytut Matematyki, Uniwersytet Jagielloński, ul. Łojasiewicza 6, 30-348 Kraków, Poland Email address: pawel.razny@uj.edu.pl
Abstract.

We give a corrected statement of [GM88, Theorem 2], which classifies smooth affine surfaces of Kodaira dimension zero, whose coordinate ring is factorial and has trivial units. Denote the class of such surfaces by 𝒮0\mathcal{S}_{0}. An infinite series of surfaces in 𝒮0\mathcal{S}_{0}, not listed in [GM88], was recently obtained by Freudenburg, Kojima and Nagamine [FKN19] as affine modifications of the plane. We complete their list to a series containing arbitrarily high-dimensional families of pairwise non-isomorphic surfaces in 𝒮0\mathcal{S}_{0}. Moreover, we classify them up to a diffeomorphism, showing that each occurs as an interior of a 44-manifold whose boundary is an exceptional surgery on a 22-bridge knot [BW01]. In particular, we show that 𝒮0\mathcal{S}_{0} contains countably many pairwise non-homeomorphic surfaces.

Key words and phrases:
affine surface, ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-fibration, log Minimal Model program, knot surgery, Kirby diagram
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary: 14R05; Secondary: 14J26, 57R65, 57M99

We work with complex algebraic varieties.

1. Introduction

The structure of smooth affine surfaces of non-general type is essentially understood, see [Miy01, Chapter III]. It can be summarized in a following way, which parallels the classical Enriques-Kodaira classification of smooth projective surfaces. Let SS be a smooth affine surface and let κ∈{−∞,0,1,2}\kappa\in\{-\infty,0,1,2\} be its Kodaira–Iitaka dimension. If κ=−∞\kappa=-\infty then SS admits a ℂ1\mathbb{C}^{1}-fibration [Miy01, III.1.3.2]. If κ=1\kappa=1 then SS has a (canonical) ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-fibration [Miy01, III.1.7.1]. The surfaces with κ=0\kappa=0 are peculiar, but understandable: they are obtained in a controlled way from some specific minimal models, see [Miy01, II.6.4].

Let 𝒮κ\mathcal{S}_{\kappa} be the class of smooth affine surfaces SS of Kodaira–Iitaka dimension κ\kappa, such that ℂ​[S]∗=ℂ∗\mathbb{C}[S]^{*}=\mathbb{C}^{*} and ℂ⁡[S]\mathbb{C}[S] is factorial, i.e. all line bundles on SS are trivial. It is known [Miy01, III.2.2.1] that S∈𝒮−∞S\in\mathcal{S}_{-\infty} if and only if S≅ℂ2S\cong\mathbb{C}^{2}. The above description of affine surfaces with κ<2\kappa<2 suggests that it is the class 𝒮0\mathcal{S}_{0} where one could look for unusual examples.

In [GM88, Theorem 2], Gurjar and Miyanishi claimed that, up to an isomorphism, there are at most two surfaces in 𝒮0\mathcal{S}_{0}. This result, however, was recently proved wrong by Freudenburg, Kojima and Nagamine [FKN19], who constructed an infinite series of pairwise non-isomorphic surfaces in 𝒮0\mathcal{S}_{0}.

The aim of this article is to complete the description of 𝒮0\mathcal{S}_{0} by proving the following theorem.

Theorem 1.1.

Let 𝒮0\mathcal{S}_{0} be the class of smooth affine surfaces SS such that the ring ℂ⁡[S]\mathbb{C}[S] is factorial, ℂ​[S]∗=ℂ∗\mathbb{C}[S]^{*}=\mathbb{C}^{*} and the logarithmic Kodaira–Iitaka dimension of SS is zero. Then S∈𝒮0S\in\mathcal{S}_{0} if and only if

S≅Sp1,p2:=Spec⁡ℂ⁡[x1,x2]​[(x2​x1−deg⁡p1−p1​(x1−1))​x1−1,(x1​x2−deg⁡p2−p2​(x2−1))​x2−1]S\cong S_{p_{1},p_{2}}:=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{C}[x_{1},x_{2}][(x_{2}x_{1}^{-\deg p_{1}}-p_{1}(x_{1}^{-1}))x_{1}^{-1},(x_{1}x_{2}^{-\deg p_{2}}-p_{2}(x_{2}^{-1}))x_{2}^{-1}]

for some monic polynomials p1,p2∈ℂ⁡[t]p_{1},p_{2}\in\mathbb{C}[t]. Moreover, Sp1,p2≇Sp1′,p2′S_{p_{1},p_{2}}\not\cong S_{p_{1}^{\prime},p_{2}^{\prime}} for {p1,p2}≠{p1′,p2′}\{p_{1},p_{2}\}\neq\{p_{1}^{\prime},p_{2}^{\prime}\}.

  2. (b)

    For n⩾1n\geqslant 1, the surface Vn=Spec⁡ℂ⁡[x,y]​[(x−1)/(xn​y−1)]V_{n}=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{C}[x,y][(x-1)/(x^{n}y-1)] constructed in [FKN19] is isomorphic to Stn−1,1S_{t^{n-1},1} via ℂ⁡[x1,x2]​[(x2−1)​x1−n,(x1−1)​x2−1]∋(x1,x2)↦(x,1−xn​y)∈ℂ⁡[x,y]​[(x−1)/(xn​y−1)]\mathbb{C}[x_{1},x_{2}][(x_{2}-1)x_{1}^{-n},(x_{1}-1)x_{2}^{-1}]\ni(x_{1},x_{2})\mapsto(x,1-x^{n}y)\in\mathbb{C}[x,y][(x-1)/(x^{n}y-1)].

In Section 4 we describe the diffeomorphism types of surfaces in 𝒮0\mathcal{S}_{0}. The result is summarized in Theorem 1.4. We refer to [GS99, §4,5] for a language of Kirby diagrams (see also Section 4A) and use the notation of [BW01] for 22-bridge knots.

The surface Sp1,p2S_{p_{1},p_{2}} from Theorem 1.1 is diffeomorphic to the interior of a 22-handlebody on a 00-framed 22-bridge knot K[2​d1,2​d2]K_{[2d_{1},2d_{2}]}, where dj=deg⁡pj+1d_{j}=\deg p_{j}+1, j∈{1,2}j\in\{1,2\}. That argument becomes more explicit once it is related to the fact that, by Theorem 1.4, MM is a 00-surgery on K[2​d1,2​d2]K_{[2d_{1},2d_{2}]}. We exploit it in Section 4C, giving a thorough geometric description of MM. The fundamental group π1​(M)=π1∞​(Sp1,p2)\pi_{1}(M)=\pi_{1}^{\infty}(S_{p_{1},p_{2}}) is computed in Proposition 4.5.

    3. (iii)

      Z=(A1∪A2)∩Sp1,p2≅ℂ1⊔ℂ1Z=(A_{1}\cup A_{2})\cap S_{p_{1},p_{2}}\cong\mathbb{C}^{1}\sqcup\mathbb{C}^{1} if p1,p2≠1p_{1},p_{2}\neq 1.

Part (a) is obtained as Corollary 2.6(c) from the uniqueness of standard boundary. To prove (b) it suffices, by [KKL20, Theorem 1.6], to describe all ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-fibrations of Sp1,p2S_{p_{1},p_{2}}: this is done in Proposition 5.5.

We now explain what is missing in the proof of [GM88, Theorem 2], and how we are going to correct it. The aforementioned result is deduced from the (partial, but sufficient) classification of almost minimal pairs of Kodaira dimension zero given in [Fuj82, §8]. For the general statement see [Koj99].

More precisely, let S∈𝒮0S\in\mathcal{S}_{0} and let (X0,D0)(X_{0},D_{0}) be a smooth completion of SS. Then by the Miyanishi’s theory of peeling (see [Miy01, p. 107] or Section 2F below), there is a sequence of birational morphisms

(X0,D0)​⟶ψ1​(X1,D1)​⟶ψ2​…​⟶ψn​(Xn,Dn),(X_{0},D_{0})\overset{\psi_{1}}{\longrightarrow}(X_{1},D_{1})\overset{\psi_{2}}{\longrightarrow}\dots\overset{\psi_{n}}{\longrightarrow}(X_{n},D_{n}),

such that (Xn,Dn)(X_{n},D_{n}) is almost minimal, hence known, and each ψi\psi_{i} is an snc-minimalization of Di−1+AD_{i-1}+A, where A⊆Xi−1A\subseteq X_{i-1} is a (−1)(-1)-curve not contained in Di−1D_{i-1} such that A⋅Di−1=1A\cdot D_{i-1}=1. The latter process is called a half-point attachment in [Fuj82, 8.15]. Therefore, to find SS it suffices to identify an (Xn,Dn)(X_{n},D_{n}) on the list in [Fuj82, 8.70] (cf. [Koj99, Proposition 1.5]), and perform suitable half-point attachments.

The proof in [GM88, Theorem 2] proceeds exactly along these lines. However, what is meant in loc. cit. by a half-point attachment is just one blowup, the contraction of AA (cf. e.g. [FZ94, Definition 4.15]). Nonetheless, if AA meets a (−2)(-2)-curve C⊆Di−1C\subseteq D_{i-1} which is not branching in Di−1D_{i-1}, then after the contraction of AA, the image of Di−1D_{i-1} is not snc-minimal, and ψi\psi_{i} should contract the image of CC, too.

This is why in [GM88] only S1,1S_{1,1} is reconstructed. Indeed, it is shown (essentially) that n=2n=2, X2=ℙ1×ℙ1X_{2}=\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{1} and D2D_{2} is a union of two vertical and two horizontal lines. But (X,D)⟶(X2,D2)(X,D)\longrightarrow(X_{2},D_{2}) is obtained by two blowups at smooth points of D2D_{2}, see Figure 1(c). The smooth completions of Sp1,p2S_{p_{1},p_{2}}, which are obtained from (X2,D2)(X_{2},D_{2}) by two sequences of blowups over D2D_{2}, see Figure 1(a), are missing.

In Section 3 we repeat the above proof, filling in the missing part. Our approach contains no essentially new ingredient. However, since the assumption S∈𝒮0S\in\mathcal{S}_{0} is substantially stronger than just κ⁡(S)=0\kappa(S)=0, we do not need to rely on the structure theorem [Fuj82, 8.70], as it is done in [GM88]. So for the convenience of the reader, we make our proof more self-contained. The only general result we refer to is the theorem of Kawamata [Kaw79, 2.2] which asserts that if κ⁡(S)=0\kappa(S)=0 then the positive part of the Zariski decomposition of KXn+DnK_{X_{n}}+D_{n} is numerically trivial, see [Miy01, II.6.2.1].

2. Preliminaries

2A. Log surfaces

We now briefly recall the language of log surfaces. For a complete introduction we refer to [Fuj82].

By a curve we mean an irreducible, reduced variety of dimension 11.

Let XX be a smooth projective surface. A curve C⊆XC\subseteq X is called an nn-curve if C≅ℙ1C\cong\mathbb{P}^{1} and C2=nC^{2}=n. In particular, a (−1)(-1)-curve is an exceptional curve of a blowup, and a 00-curve is a fiber of a ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}-fibration.

Let DD be an effective ℚ\mathbb{Q}-divisor on XX. By a component of DD we always mean an irreducible component. The number of components of DD is denoted by #​D\#D. The branching number of a component C⊆DC\subseteq D is

βD​(C)=C⋅(D−C).\beta_{D}(C)=C\cdot(D-C).

We say that CC is a tip of DD if βDred​(C)=1\beta_{D_{\mathrm{red}}}(C)=1, and branching in DD if βDred​(C)⩾3\beta_{D_{\mathrm{red}}}(C)\geqslant 3.

Assume that DD is simple normal crossing (snc), that is, DD is reduced, all components of DD are smooth and meet transversally, at most two at each point. A (−1)(-1)-curve C⊆DC\subseteq D is called superfluous if 1⩽βD​(C)⩽21\leqslant\beta_{D}(C)\leqslant 2 and CC meets each component of DD at most once: in other words, after contraction of CC, the image of DD remains snc. We say that DD is snc-minimal if it contains no superfluous (−1)(-1)-curves. An snc-minimalization of DD is the contraction of all superfluous (−1)(-1)-curves in DD and its images.

Assume further that DD has connected support and βD​(C)⩽2\beta_{D}(C)\leqslant 2 for all components CC of DD. We say that DD is a chain if at least one inequality is strict, otherwise we say that DD is circular. We order the components T1,…,TmT_{1},\dots,T_{m} of DD in such a way that Ti⋅Ti+1=1T_{i}\cdot T_{i+1}=1 for i∈{1,…,m−1}i\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}, and T1T_{1} is a tip of DD in case DD is a chain. The sequence of integers (−T12,…,−Tm2)(-T_{1}^{2},\dots,-T_{m}^{2}) is then called a type of DD. We often abuse notation and write

D=[−T12,…,−Tm2]​ if D is a chain and ​D=((,,,,,))​ if D is circular.D=[-T_{1}^{2},\dots,-T_{m}^{2}]\mbox{ if $D$ is a chain and }D=(\!(-T_{1}^{2},\dots,-T_{m}^{2})\!)\mbox{ if $D$ is circular}.

A sequence consisting of an integer aa repeated kk times will be abbreviated as (a)k(a)_{k}.

An effective divisor DD is called a tree if DredD_{\mathrm{red}} is snc and has no circular subdivisor. A fork is a tree with exactly one branching component and three maximal twigs. A rational tree (chain, fork…) is a tree (chain, fork…) whose components are all rational.

We say that a reduced divisor D=∑DiD=\sum D_{i} is negative definite if its intersection matrix [Di⋅Dj]1⩽i,j⩽r[D_{i}\cdot D_{j}]_{1\leqslant i,j\leqslant r} is.

Let again DD be an snc divisor. A chain T⊆DT\subseteq D is a twig of DD if it contains a tip of DD and its components are non-branching in DD. We order a twig in such a way that its first component is a tip of DD. A twig is called admissible if all its components are rational and have self-intersection number at most −2-2. An (admissible) twig of DD is maximal if it is maximal in the set of (admissible) twigs ordered by inclusion of supports. A (−2)(-2)-twig is a twig whose components are (−2)(-2)-curves.

Let TT be an admissible twig of DD. Then TT is negative definite, so there is a unique ℚ\mathbb{Q}-divisor BkD⁡(T)⩽T\operatorname{Bk}_{D}(T)\leqslant T, called the bark of TT, such that for every component T0T_{0} of TT

T0⋅BkD⁡(T)=T0⋅(KX+D),T_{0}\cdot\operatorname{Bk}_{D}(T)=T_{0}\cdot(K_{X}+D),

that is, T0⋅BkD⁡(T)=−1T_{0}\cdot\operatorname{Bk}_{D}(T)=-1 if T0T_{0} is a tip of DD and T0⋅BkD⁡(T)=0T_{0}\cdot\operatorname{Bk}_{D}(T)=0 otherwise. An important result for the theory of peeling asserts that the coefficients of BkD⁡(T)\operatorname{Bk}_{D}(T) are strictly between 00 and 11 [Miy01, II.3.3].

Assume that DD is a connected snc-minimal divisor which is not negative definite. Then Bk⁡D\operatorname{Bk}D is defined as the sum of barks of all maximal admissible twigs of DD. We put D#=D−Bk⁡DD^{\#}=D-\operatorname{Bk}D.

Let DD be an snc divisor on XX. We say that a blowup X′⟶XX^{\prime}\longrightarrow X at a point p∈Dp\in D is outer with respect to DD if pp is a smooth point of DD, otherwise it is called inner. We say that a birational map X⇢YX\dashrightarrow Y touches a divisor if it is not an isomorphism in any of its neighborhoods.

A log smooth pair (X,D)(X,D) consists of a smooth projective surface XX and an snc divisor DD on XX. Any smooth surface SS admits a log smooth completion, that is, a log smooth pair (X,D)(X,D) such that S≅X∖DS\cong X\setminus D. We say that such a completion is minimal if it does not dominate birationally any other log smooth completion, or, equivalently, if DD is snc-minimal.

2B. Affine surfaces whose coordinate rings are factorial and have trivial units

For a divisor DD on a smooth surface XX, we denote by ℤ⁡[D]\mathbb{Z}[D] the free abelian group whose basis is the set of components of DD. There is a natural group homomorphism ℤ⁡[D]⟶Pic⁡(X)\mathbb{Z}[D]\longrightarrow\operatorname{Pic}(X). The following lemma is well known, cf. [Fuj82, 1.17] or [GM88, Lemma 2.2].

Lemma 2.1 (Criterion for S∈𝒮κS\in\mathcal{S}_{\kappa}).

Let (X,D)(X,D) be a smooth completion of a smooth affine surface SS.

  1. (a)

    ℂ⁡[S]\mathbb{C}[S] is a UFD if and only if ℤ⁡[D]⟶Pic⁡(X)\mathbb{Z}[D]\longrightarrow\operatorname{Pic}(X) is surjective.

  2. (b)

    ℂ​[S]∗=ℂ∗\mathbb{C}[S]^{*}=\mathbb{C}^{*} if and only if ℤ⁡[D]⟶Pic⁡(X)\mathbb{Z}[D]\longrightarrow\operatorname{Pic}(X) is injective.

Assume that S∈𝒮κS\in\mathcal{S}_{\kappa}. Then ℤ⁡[D]=Pic⁡(X)=NS⁡(X)\mathbb{Z}[D]=\operatorname{Pic}(X)=\operatorname{NS}(X) and q⁡(X)=0q(X)=0. If κ<2\kappa<2 then XX is rational.

(a) By [Har77, II.6.2], ℂ⁡[S]\mathbb{C}[S] is factorial if and only if the divisor class group Cl⁡(S)\mathrm{Cl}(S) of SS is trivial. It follows from [Har77, II.6.5(c)] that Cl⁡(S)\mathrm{Cl}(S) is the cokernel of the natural map ℤ⁡[D]⟶Cl⁡(X)\mathbb{Z}[D]\longrightarrow\mathrm{Cl}(X). Eventually, Cl⁡(X)=Pic⁡(X)\mathrm{Cl}(X)=\operatorname{Pic}(X) because XX is smooth [Har77, II.6.16].

(b) A regular function on SS is invertible if and only if it extends to f∈ℂ⁡(X)f\in\mathbb{C}(X) with all zeros and poles in DD, that is, with div⁡(f)∈ℤ⁡[D]\mathrm{div}(f)\in\mathbb{Z}[D]. Two rational functions on XX with the same divisor differ by an element of 𝒪X​(X)∗=ℂ∗\mathcal{O}_{X}(X)^{*}=\mathbb{C}^{*}, so f↦div⁡(f)f\mapsto\mathrm{div}(f) gives an isomorphism of ℂ​[S]∗/ℂ∗\mathbb{C}[S]^{*}/\mathbb{C}^{*} with the kernel of ℤ⁡[D]⟶Pic⁡(X)\mathbb{Z}[D]\longrightarrow\operatorname{Pic}(X).

For the remaining part, we follow [GM88, Lemma 2.2]. Assume that S∈𝒮κS\in\mathcal{S}_{\kappa}. Then (a), (b) give ℤ⁡[D]=Pic⁡(X)\mathbb{Z}[D]=\operatorname{Pic}(X). The exponential sequence induces an exact sequence

0⟶H1​(X,ℤ)⟶H1​(X,𝒪X)⟶Pic⁡(X)⟶H2​(X,ℤ).0\longrightarrow H^{1}(X,\mathbb{Z})\longrightarrow H^{1}(X,\mathcal{O}_{X})\longrightarrow\operatorname{Pic}(X)\longrightarrow H^{2}(X,\mathbb{Z}).

Since H1​(X,𝒪X)H^{1}(X,\mathcal{O}_{X}) is a vector space over ℂ\mathbb{C}, and by (a) Pic⁡(X)\operatorname{Pic}(X) is a finitely generated abelian group, we obtain q⁡(X)=h1​(X,𝒪X)=0q(X)=h^{1}(X,\mathcal{O}_{X})=0 and that Pic⁡(X)⟶H2​(X,ℤ)\operatorname{Pic}(X)\longrightarrow H^{2}(X,\mathbb{Z}) is injective, i.e. Pic⁡(X)=NS⁡(X)\operatorname{Pic}(X)=\operatorname{NS}(X). Now to prove that XX is rational, it remains to show that pg​(X)=0p_{g}(X)=0 [Har77, IV.6.2]. Assume κ<2\kappa<2. Because SS is affine, DD supports an effective ample divisor, so if |KX|≠∅|K_{X}|\neq\emptyset then for m≫0m\gg 0 we have h0​(m⁡(KX+D))∼m2h^{0}(m(K_{X}+D))\sim m^{2}, hence κ=2\kappa=2; a contradiction. ∎

Remark 2.2.

Lemma 2.1(a) implies that an open affine subset of a smooth factorial surface is factorial, and that the converse holds if and only if its complement is a principal divisor. This is a special case of the Nagata lemma, see e.g. [Eis95, Lemma 19.20]

2C. ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}-fibrations

A fibration of a smooth surface SS is a surjective morphism onto a curve whose general fiber is irreducible and reduced. A curve on SS is called vertical (resp. horizontal) if C⋅F=0C\cdot F=0 (resp. C⋅F>0C\cdot F>0) for a fiber FF; it is called an nn-section if C⋅F=nC\cdot F=n. Any divisor DD decomposes uniquely as D=Dvert+DhorD=D_{\mathrm{vert}}+D_{\mathrm{hor}}, where all components of DvertD_{\mathrm{vert}} are vertical and all components of DhorD_{\mathrm{hor}} are horizontal.

A ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}- (resp. ℂ1\mathbb{C}^{1}-, ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-) fibration is a fibration whose general fiber is isomorphic to ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} (resp. ℂ1\mathbb{C}^{1}, ℂ∗:=ℂ1∖{0}\mathbb{C}^{*}:=\mathbb{C}^{1}\setminus\{0\}). A fiber not isomorphic to a general one will be called degenerate.

The surfaces in 𝒮0\mathcal{S}_{0} do not admit ℂ1\mathbb{C}^{1}-fibrations by the Iitaka Easy Addition Theorem [Iit82, Theorem 11.9], but they admit plenty of ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-fibrations (eg. produced by Lemma 3.1(a)), which we will use in Proposition 5.5(c) as first integrals for complete algebraic vector fields, see [KKL20, Theorem 1.6]. The structure of ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-fibrations is well described in [Fuj82, §7], however, for our purposes it will be more convenient to study them directly, by completing them to ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}-fibrations.

Let FF be a degenerate fiber of a ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}-fibration of a smooth projective surface. Then FF is obtained from a 00-curve by a sequence of blowups, hence its geometry is easy to understand, see eg. [Fuj82, §4]. In particular, FF is a rational tree with no branching (−1)(-1)-curves; moreover, if a (−1)(-1)-curve has multiplicity 11 in FF then it is a tip of FF, and FF contains another (−1)(-1)-curve [Fuj82, 7.3].

The following observation, see [Fuj82, 7.14(1)], will be used several times.

Lemma 2.4 (our ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-fibrations are untwisted).

Let (X,D)(X,D) be a log smooth completion of a smooth affine surface SS such that ℂ⁡[S]\mathbb{C}[S] is a UFD. Let H1,…,HrH_{1},\dots,H_{r} be all components of DhorD_{\mathrm{hor}} for some ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}-fibration of XX. Put hj=Hj⋅Fh_{j}=H_{j}\cdot F for a fiber FF. Then gcd⁡(h1,…,hr)=1\gcd(h_{1},\dots,h_{r})=1.

By Tsen’s theorem, XX contains a 11-section HH. By Lemma 2.1(a), H≡V+∑j=1raj​HjH\equiv V+\sum_{j=1}^{r}a_{j}H_{j} for some vertical VV and a1,…,ar∈ℤa_{1},\dots,a_{r}\in\mathbb{Z}. Intersecting with FF gives 1=∑j=1raj​hj1=\sum_{j=1}^{r}a_{j}h_{j}, so gcd⁡(h1,…,hr)=1\gcd(h_{1},\dots,h_{r})=1. ∎

2D. Standard completions and elementary transformations

A minimal log smooth completion of an open surface may not be unique. However, [FKZ07, Definition 2.13] distinguishes a class of standard completions, which gives a convenient tool to tell affine surfaces apart. We now recall this definition. A rational chain is standard if it is of type

[(0)2​k+1]or[(0)2​k,a1,…,al]for some integers ​k,l⩾0​ and ​a1,…,al⩾2.[(0)_{2k+1}]\quad\mbox{or}\quad[(0)_{2k},a_{1},\dots,a_{l}]\quad\mbox{for some integers }k,l\geqslant 0\mbox{ and }a_{1},\dots,a_{l}\geqslant 2.

A rational circular divisor is standard if it is of type

((,,,,,,,))​ or ​(((0)k,a))​ or ​((,,,,,))for some ​k,l⩾0,a⩾0​ and ​a,a1,…,al⩾2.(\!((0)_{2k},a_{1},\dots,a_{l})\!)\mbox{ or }(\!((0)_{k},a)\!)\mbox{ or }(\!((0)_{2k},1,1)\!)\quad\mbox{for some }k,l\geqslant 0,\ a\geqslant 0\mbox{ and }a,a_{1},\dots,a_{l}\geqslant 2.

Let now DD be any snc divisor, and let BB be the sum of all components of DD which are either branching or non-rational; so every connected component of D−BD-B is rational, chain or circular. We say that DD is standard if every connected component of D−BD-B is standard in the above sense. A log smooth completion (X,D)(X,D) is standard if DD is. Note that the log smooth completions of Sp1,p2S_{p_{1},p_{2}} in Figure 1 are standard.

Let DD be an snc divisor on XX, and let C⊆DC\subseteq D be a non-branching 00-curve. If βD​(C)=2\beta_{D}(C)=2 choose p∈C∩(D−C)p\in C\cap(D-C), otherwise let pp be any point of CC. A flow (or elementary transformation) on CC is the birational map (X,D)⇢(X′,D′)(X,D)\dashrightarrow(X^{\prime},D^{\prime}), where D′D^{\prime} is the reduced total transform of DD, defined as a blowup at pp, followed by the contraction of the proper transform of CC. We remark that in Section 5 we will use the word “flow” in its standard meaning, i.e. flow of a vector field: this will lead to no confusion.

Let φ:(X,D)⇢(X′,D′)\varphi\colon(X,D)\dashrightarrow(X^{\prime},D^{\prime}) be a flow on C⊆DC\subseteq D. Then φ|X∖D:X∖D⟶X′∖D′\varphi|_{X\setminus D}\colon X\setminus D\longrightarrow X^{\prime}\setminus D^{\prime} is an isomorphism. In particular, if the components of DD generate Pic⁡(X)\operatorname{Pic}(X) (respectively, are ℤ\mathbb{Z}-linearly independent in Pic⁡(X)\operatorname{Pic}(X)), then by Lemma 2.1 the same is true for the components of D′D^{\prime} in Pic⁡(X′)\operatorname{Pic}(X^{\prime}). Moreover, φ\varphi does not touch components of DD other than CC and the components of DD meeting CC. If CC is not a tip of DD, then φ\varphi replaces a subchain [a,0,b]⊆D[a,0,b]\subseteq D, whose middle component is CC, by [a+1,0,b−1]⊆D′[a+1,0,b-1]\subseteq D^{\prime}.

We are ready to formulate the result used to distinguish the surfaces Sp1,p2S_{p_{1},p_{2}} for different {p1,p2}\{p_{1},p_{2}\}.

Lemma 2.5 ([FKZ07, Corollary 3.36]).

Any smooth affine surface admits a standard log smooth completion. Any two such completions differ by a sequence of flows on some 00-curves in the boundary.

Lemma 2.8 ([Fuj82, 6.13], cf. [FZ94, Lemma 4.14]).

2E. Graph 33-manifolds and their normal forms

An important topological invariant of an affine surface SS is its fundamental group at infinity, π1∞​(S):=lim←⁡π1​(S∖K)\pi_{1}^{\infty}(S):=\varprojlim\pi_{1}(S\setminus K), where lim←\varprojlim runs over all compact K⊆SK\subseteq S. If (X,D)(X,D) is a log smooth completion of SS, then π1∞​(S)=π1​(M)\pi_{1}^{\infty}(S)=\pi_{1}(M), where MM is the boundary of a nice tubular neighborhood of DD, constructed in [Mum61] as a plumbed manifold whose graph is the dual graph of DD, see [GS99, 4.6.2]. More precisely, Tub⁡(D)\mathrm{Tub}(D) is a union, taken over components CC of DD, of disk bundles ξC\xi_{C} with Euler numbers C2C^{2}, where for any component C′C^{\prime} of DD meeting CC, a fiber of ξC\xi_{C} over C∩C′C\cap C^{\prime} is glued to a neighborhood of C∩C′C\cap C^{\prime} in CC.

For a general introduction to 33-manifolds we refer to [Hat07, AFW15]. We denote by 𝕊k\mathbb{S}^{k}, 𝔻k\mathbb{D}^{k} the (real) kk-dimensional sphere and disk, respectively, and by 𝕋k=(𝕊1)k\mathbb{T}^{k}=(\mathbb{S}^{1})^{k} the kk-dimensional torus. We say that a 33-manifold is prime if it cannot be written as a connected sum of two 33-manifolds other than 𝕊3\mathbb{S}^{3}, and irreducible if any embedded 𝕊2\mathbb{S}^{2} bounds a ball. A prime, oriented 33-manifold is either irreducible or 𝕊1×𝕊2\mathbb{S}^{1}\times\mathbb{S}^{2}.

If MM is prime, and not a lens space (which will be the case for S=Sp1,p2S=S_{p_{1},p_{2}}), then π1​(M)\pi_{1}(M) determines MM uniquely, up to a diffeomorphism [AFW15, Theorem 2.1.2]. Therefore, in this case to distinguish the homeomorphism type of SS at infinity, it suffices to describe π1​(M)\pi_{1}(M), which, in turn, is given by the graph of DD, once put in a normal form [Neu81, Theorem 4.2]. The definition of normal form is similar to the one of standard boundary, but requires some more flexibility to allow more operations between 33-manifolds than just blowing up and down. We now recall the definition of graph 33-manifolds following [Neu81]. We refer to [EN85] for details and relation to the JSJ-decomposition (graph manifolds are exactly those for which the latter consists only of Seifert fibered spaces: we compute it for our MM in Proposition 4.7).

A graph manifold is a 33-manifold which is a union of 𝕊1\mathbb{S}^{1}-bundles over compact surfaces, glued according to some graph, as follows. An 𝕊1\mathbb{S}^{1}-bundle over CC with Euler number ee is represented by a vertex of weight ee and two additional numbers gg, rr, where gg is the genus of CC (g<0g<0 if CC is non-orientable) and r=b0​(∂C)r=b_{0}(\partial C). They are skipped whenever both are zero, i.e. C≅ℙ1C\cong\mathbb{P}^{1}. An edge between two vertices v1v_{1}, v2v_{2} represents gluing of a fiber of v1v_{1} to a small loop around a point in a base of v2v_{2}, and vice versa. Multiple edges and loops are allowed. An edge is labeled by “++” if the gluing respects the chosen orientations, and “−-” if it reverses both of them. Clearly, reversing the sign of all edges adjacent to a single vertex, or of any edge adjacent to a vertex with g<0g<0, does not change the manifold. Hence we will label only the edges contained in circular subgraphs with no vertices of g<0g<0, see [Neu81, p. 304].

For example, the boundary MM from [Mum61], described above, is a graph manifold associated to the dual graph of DD, with all edges labeled with “++”. For such graph, we use the notions of branching numbers, chains, twigs as in Section 2A, a vertex being “rational” if g=r=0g=r=0.

A connected, rational graph Γ\Gamma is normal if the following three conditions hold. First, all non-branching vertices of Γ\Gamma have weights at most −2-2. Second, if a vertex with β=3\beta=3 meets two twigs of type [2][2] then Γ\Gamma is a fork. Third, if Γ=(((2)k))\Gamma=(\!((2)_{k})\!) for some k>0k>0 then at least two edges are labeled with “−-”. To extend this definition to non-rational graphs, one needs to exclude some additional special cases, see [Neu81, §4]. We will not need this extension. In general, a graph is normal if all its connected components are.

For a graph 33-manifold NN, [Neu81, Theorem 4.1] gives an algorithm to reduce its graph to a normal form, which we denote by Γ⁡(N)\Gamma(N). This algorithm uses certain operations R0–R8 defined in Proposition 2.1 loc. cit, which do not change the graph manifold. Among these, R1 is blowing down a vertex with weight ±1\pm 1, and R3 is an “absorption” of a cylinder (𝔻1×𝕊1)×𝕊1(\mathbb{D}^{1}\times\mathbb{S}^{1})\times\mathbb{S}^{1} corresponding to a rational vertex of weight 00 and β=2\beta=2. The graph Γ⁡(−N)\Gamma(-N) can be directly computed from Γ⁡(N)\Gamma(N) using [Neu81, Theorem 7.1].

Now we can state the main result of [Neu81] used to distinguish π1∞​(Sp1,p2)\pi_{1}^{\infty}(S_{p_{1},p_{2}}) for different degrees of pjp_{j}.

Lemma 2.9 ([Neu81, Theorems 4.2, 4.3]).

Let N,N′N,N^{\prime} be graph 33-manifolds.

  1. (a)

    Γ⁡(N)=Γ⁡(N′)\Gamma(N)=\Gamma(N^{\prime}) if and only if NN and N′N^{\prime} are orientation-preserving diffeomorphic.

  2. (b)

    If Γ\Gamma is connected then NN is prime.

Corollary 2.10.

The surfaces Sp1,p2S_{p_{1},p_{2}} and Sp1′,p2′S_{p_{1}^{\prime},p_{2}^{\prime}} are not homeomorphic for {deg⁡p1,deg⁡p2}≠{deg⁡p1′,deg⁡p2′}\{\deg p_{1},\deg p_{2}\}\neq\{\deg p_{1}^{\prime},\deg p_{2}^{\prime}\}.

For Sp1,p2S_{p_{1},p_{2}} and Sp1′,p2′S_{p_{1}^{\prime},p_{2}^{\prime}}, {deg⁡p1,deg⁡p2}≠{deg⁡p1′,deg⁡p2′}\{\deg p_{1},\deg p_{2}\}\neq\{\deg p_{1}^{\prime},\deg p_{2}^{\prime}\} let MM, M′M^{\prime} be a boundary of tubular neighborhoods of respective D⊆XD\subseteq X as in Construction 1.3. Such MM is a graph manifold represented by Figure 4(a). Absorption (move R3 in [Neu81]) of a vertex corresponding to L1,∞L_{1,\infty} reduces it to a graph in Figure 4(b). It is in normal form if p1,p2≠1p_{1},p_{2}\neq 1. If, say, p1=1p_{1}=1 then the normal form is obtained by blowing down (move R1) the vertex corresponding to L1,0L_{1,0}. If p2≠1p_{2}\neq 1, then the resulting graph in Figure 4(c) is normal, otherwise it needs to be replaced by a standard graph of a Seifert fiber space (move R7). In our case this graph is a graph E9E_{9}, which after orientation reversing gives the one in Figure 4(d), cf. Proposition 4.7(c) and [Neu81, p. 309].

Hence Γ⁡(M)≠Γ⁡(M′)\Gamma(M)\neq\Gamma(M^{\prime}), so by Lemma 2.9(a) MM is not orientation-preserving diffeomorphic to M′M^{\prime}. Reversing orientation in Figures 44(b)-4(c) inverts the edge signs and replaces a twig [(2)d][(2)_{d}] with [d+2][d+2], so the resulting graph is different from the previous ones. Therefore, M≇diffeoM′M\not\cong_{\mathrm{diffeo}}M^{\prime}, so M≇homeoM′M\not\cong_{\mathrm{homeo}}M^{\prime}, see [AFW15, 1.1]. Because Γ⁡(M)\Gamma(M) is connected and not a rational chain, MM is prime, and not a lens space (see [Neu81, 6.1] for lens space graphs), so by [AFW15, 2.1.2] π1​(M)≇π1​(M′)\pi_{1}(M)\not\cong\pi_{1}(M^{\prime}). The result follows because π1∞​(Sp1,p2)=π1​(M)\pi_{1}^{\infty}(S_{p_{1},p_{2}})=\pi_{1}(M) [Mum61]. ∎

2F. Almost minimal models

We now recall the construction of an almost minimal model for a log smooth pair (X,D)(X,D). We consider only the case when X∖DX\setminus D is affine, for a complete treatment we refer to [Miy01, §3], see p. 107 loc. cit. for a summary. The exposition here is based on [Pal19, §3].

The motivation for this construction to get an explicit description of a log MMP run for the pair (X,D)(X,D), such that the log terminal singularities on the image of (X,D)(X,D) are introduced as late as possible: in fact, an almost minimal model is a log resolution of the minimal model in the sense of Mori. Having understood the latter, one can use this theory to reconstruct the initial pair (X,D)(X,D).

The almost minimal model will be created by iterating birational morphisms of the following type.

Definition 2.11 (half-point attachment, cf. [Fuj82]).

Let (X,D)(X,D) be a log smooth pair. Assume that

(2.1) A⊆X​ is a ​(−1)​-curve such that ​A⊈D​ and ​A⋅D=1.A\subseteq X\mbox{ is a }(-1)\mbox{-curve such that }A\not\subseteq D\mbox{ and }A\cdot D=1.

The composition of the contraction of AA and new superfluous (−1)(-1)-curves in the subsequent images of DD:

φA:(X,D)⟶(X′,D′),\varphi_{A}\colon(X,D)\longrightarrow(X^{\prime},D^{\prime}),

where D′=(φA)∗​DD^{\prime}=(\varphi_{A})_{*}D, is called a half-point attachment (of AA).

Remark.

In general, φA\varphi_{A} is not uniquely determined by AA. Indeed, it may happen that after some contraction within φA\varphi_{A}, there appear two superfluous (−1)(-1)-curves. For example, if AA meets the middle component T′T^{\prime} of a subchain T=[2,2,2]T=[2,2,2] of DD, whose components are non-branching in DD, then after the contraction of A+T′A+T^{\prime}, both components of the image of TT are superfluous (−1)(-1)-curves in the image of DD, but only one of them can be contracted.

However, such ambiguity never happens if ℂ⁡[X∖D]\mathbb{C}[X\setminus D] is a UFD. Indeed, Lemma 3.1(b) shows that in this case φA\varphi_{A} contracts exactly AA and a maximal (−2)(-2)-twig of DD meeting AA (if such occurs).

Lemma 2.12.

Let (X,D)⟶(X′,D′)(X,D)\longrightarrow(X^{\prime},D^{\prime}) be a half-point attachment. Then for all m⩾0m\geqslant 0 we have h0​(m⁡(KX′+D′))=h0​(m⁡(KX+D))h^{0}(m(K_{X^{\prime}}+D^{\prime}))=h^{0}(m(K_{X}+D)). In particular, κ⁡(X′∖D′)=κ⁡(X∖D)\kappa(X^{\prime}\setminus D^{\prime})=\kappa(X\setminus D).

Let AA be as in (2.1). We have A⋅(KX+D+A)=−1<0A\cdot(K_{X}+D+A)=-1<0, so for any m>0m>0, m​AmA is in the fixed locus of |m⁡(KX+D+A)||m(K_{X}+D+A)|. Therefore, |m⁡(KX+D)|≅|m⁡(KX+D+A)|≅|m⁡(KX′+D′)||m(K_{X}+D)|\cong|m(K_{X}+D+A)|\cong|m(K_{X^{\prime}}+D^{\prime})| because X⟶X′X\longrightarrow X^{\prime} contracts only components of D+AD+A. ∎

Corollary 2.13.

The surfaces Sp1,p2S_{p_{1},p_{2}} from Theorem 1.1 are in 𝒮0\mathcal{S}_{0}.

4. Diffeomorphism type of Sp1,p2S_{p_{1},p_{2}}

In this section we prove Theorem 1.4. To this end, we need to translate Construction 1.3 to the language of Kirby calculus, where blowing up corresponds to attaching handles. We give a quick overview of handlebodies and Kirby diagrams in Section 4A. In Proposition 4.3 we show that Construction 1.3 amounts to attaching two 22-handles to 𝕋2×𝔻2\mathbb{T}^{2}\times\mathbb{D}^{2}, whose interior is identified with ℂ∗×ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}\times\mathbb{C}^{*}, see Figure 3. Theorem 1.4 follows by sliding its 22-handle over the attached ones. The boundary MM of the obtained 44-manifold is a 00-surgery on the knot KK from Figure 2. It is interesting to note that this is one of the few exceptional surgeries on KK, classified in [BW01]. More precisely, while all but finitely many surgeries on KK are hyperbolic, MM contains incompressible tori. Decomposition of MM along these tori is described in Proposition 4.7. While interesting in its own right, it gives another way to distinguish Sp1,p2S_{p_{1},p_{2}}, for different {deg⁡p1,deg⁡p2}\{\deg p_{1},\deg p_{2}\}.

We begin with the following observation.

For every p1,p2p_{1},p_{2}, Sp1,p2S_{p_{1},p_{2}} is homotopically equivalent to 𝕊2\mathbb{S}^{2}.

This modification replaces {x1x2=0}⊆ℂ2\{x_{1}x_{2}=0\}\subseteq\mathbb{C}^{2}, which is contractible, by the affine part of A1+A2A_{1}+A_{2}, which is a disjoint union of two copies of ℂ1\mathbb{C}^{1}. Hence etop​(S)=etop​(ℂ2)−1+2=2e_{\mathrm{top}}(S)=e_{\mathrm{top}}(\mathbb{C}^{2})-1+2=2. Because SS, being Stein, has a homotopy type of a CW-complex of (real) dimension two [GS99, 11.2.6], it follows that Hi​(S,ℤ)=ℤH_{i}(S,\mathbb{Z})=\mathbb{Z} for i=2i=2 and 00 for i>2i>2. Thus SS has weak homotopy type of 𝕊2\mathbb{S}^{2}. Applying the Whitehead theorem to the continuous map 𝕊2⟶S\mathbb{S}^{2}\longrightarrow S given by a generator of π2​(S)=H2​(S,ℤ)=ℤ\pi_{2}(S)=H_{2}(S;\mathbb{Z})=\mathbb{Z}, we infer that 𝕊2≃htpS\mathbb{S}^{2}\simeq_{\mathrm{htp}}S, as claimed. ∎

4A. Overview of Kirby calculus

We now briefly recall the language of Kirby diagrams of 44-manifolds, for a complete treatment see [GS99, §4-5]. A (44-dimensional) kk-handle hh for k∈{0,…,4}k\in\{0,\dots,4\} is a copy of 𝔻k×𝔻4−k\mathbb{D}^{k}\times\mathbb{D}^{4-k} attached to a boundary of a 44-manifold VV via an embedding φ:∂𝔻k×𝔻4−k⟶∂V\varphi\colon\partial\mathbb{D}^{k}\times\mathbb{D}^{4-k}\longrightarrow\partial V. The images of ∂𝔻k×0\partial\mathbb{D}^{k}\times 0 and 0×∂𝔻4−k0\times\partial\mathbb{D}^{4-k} are called the attaching and belt spheres of hh, the image of 𝔻k×0\mathbb{D}^{k}\times 0 is called the core of hh, see [GS99, Fig. 4.1]. Smoothing corners gives a 44-manifold V∪φhV\cup_{\varphi}h which depends only on the attaching sphere of hh and, if k=2k=2, on the integer called framing of hh, which equals the linking number of its attaching circle and its push-off along a transverse vector field [GS99, 4.1, 4.5]. For example, blowing up is the same as attaching a 22-handle with framing −1-1 [GS99, p. 150].

Any 44-manifold VV can be obtained from 𝔻4\mathbb{D}^{4} by attaching handles of increasing index. There are two ways of modifying such handle-decomposition without changing the diffeomorphism type of VV. First, if the attaching sphere of a kk-handle meets the belt sphere of a (k−1)(k-1)-handle transversally in a single point, these two handles can be canceled [GS99, 4.2.9]. Second, a 22-handle hh can be slid over a 22-handle h0h_{0} by pushing the attaching circle of hh through the belt circle of h0h_{0} [GS99, 4.2.10]. We use the same letter to denote a handle before and after the slide.

A handle-decomposition of VV is encoded by a Kirby diagram, which is a (decorated) link in 𝕊3\mathbb{S}^{3}, i.e. in the boundary of the initial 00-handle. A 22-handle is represented by its attaching circle with a framing coefficient. Attaching a 11-handle to VV is the same as drilling a tubular neighborhood of a properly embedded 𝔻2⊆V\mathbb{D}^{2}\subseteq V [GS99, p. 168], so it is represented by a circle ∂𝔻2⊆∂V\partial\mathbb{D}^{2}\subseteq\partial V, with a dot to distinguish it from a 22-handle. All dotted circles in a Kirby diagram form an unlink. Once 11- and 22-handles are attached, there is usually (e.g. if VV is closed or ∂V\partial V is connected and VV is simply connected, which is our case) a unique way to attach the remaining ones [GS99, p. 148], so they are not drawn. We use the same letters for handles and corresponding knots in the diagram.

For example, a diagram consisting of one unknot with coefficient ee represents a 𝔻2\mathbb{D}^{2}-bundle over 𝕊2\mathbb{S}^{2} of Euler number ee [GS99, Fig. 4.20]. The diagram in Figure 3 without the leftmost and rightmost circle represents 𝕋2×𝔻2\mathbb{T}^{2}\times\mathbb{D}^{2}, see [GS99, Fig. 4.36]. Indeed, attaching the 11-handles gives (𝕋2∖{disk})×𝔻2(\mathbb{T}^{2}\setminus\{\mbox{disk}\})\times\mathbb{D}^{2}, whose fundamental group is freely generated by loops based in the initial 00-handle and going along the cores of the 11-handles. The 22-handle, attached along their commutator, caps off the puncture.

Handle cancellation and sliding is represented on the Kirby diagram as follows. First, if a dotted circle meets only one non-dotted circle, once, then the corresponding 11- and 22-handle cancel [GS99, Fig. 5.38]. Second, sliding a 22-handle tt over t0t_{0} replaces tt by its band-sum with a parallel copy t~0\widetilde{t}_{0} of t0t_{0} [GS99, Fig. 5.4]. More precisely, choose an arc in tt and t~0\widetilde{t}_{0} and connect their endpoints such that the obtained “square” bounds a band which is disjoint from the rest of the diagram. Recall that ℓ​k​(t0,t~0)\ell k(t_{0},\widetilde{t}_{0}) is the framing of t0t_{0}. The new framing of tt is the sum of framings of tt and t0t_{0} plus 2​ℓ​k​(t,t0)2\ell k(t,t_{0}) [GS99, p. 142]. It is important to remember that the orientations of tt and t~0\widetilde{t}_{0} should match. We denote by −t-t the knot tt taken with opposite orientation. The components of a standard Hopf link drawn as in the left of Figure 7 are always meant to have counterclockwise orientation and linking number +1+1.

4C. Computation of π1∞​(Sp1,p2)\pi_{1}^{\infty}(S_{p_{1},p_{2}}) and a relation with knot surgeries

Proposition 4.3 allows us to compute the fundamental group of VV (which is trivial by Proposition 4.1), and, more interestingly, that of MM, which equals π1∞​(S)\pi_{1}^{\infty}(S), see [Mum61].

Proposition 4.5.

The fundamental group at infinity of SS has a presentation

Let γ1,γ2,λ∈π1​(∂(𝕋2×𝔻2))=π1​(𝕋3)\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\lambda\in\pi_{1}(\partial(\mathbb{T}^{2}\times\mathbb{D}^{2}))=\pi_{1}(\mathbb{T}^{3}) be the standard generators. Remark 4.6.

The presentation (4.1) can also be obtained from the plumbing construction in [Mum61], see Section 2E. If DD is a tree, [Mum61] shows how to calculate π1​(M)\pi_{1}(M) in terms of fibers of the plumbed 𝕊1\mathbb{S}^{1}-bundles, using van Kampen theorem. For our DD, one needs to use the van Kampen theorem for groupoids [Bro67], say, to glue ∂Tub⁡(L1,∞+L2,∞)\partial\mathrm{Tub}(L_{1,\infty}+L_{2,\infty}) to the rest of ∂Tub⁡(D)\partial\mathrm{Tub}(D) along two disjoint plumbing tori, each containing a base point. This gives the additional generator λ\lambda, which is the sum of paths joining the two base points in each of the glued pieces. In this interpretation, γj\gamma_{j} is the fiber over Lj,0L_{j,0}. Indeed, in the proof of Proposition 4.3 it was drawn parallel to the boundary of a disk corresponding to Tj,dj−1T_{j,d_{j}-1}, which goes once around Lj,0L_{j,0}. In turn, δj\delta_{j} is a fiber over Tj,1T_{j,1}, that is, a singular fiber of a lens space L⁡(1,dj)L(1,d_{j}) attached to ∂Tub⁡(Lj,0)\partial\mathrm{Tub}(L_{j,0}).

In the proof of Corollary 2.10, we have essentially seen the JSJ decomposition of MM. We will now show how to see it from the above description of MM, as a 00-surgery on K[2​d1,2​d2]K_{[2d_{1},2d_{2}]}. In order to settle the notation, we recall the basic definitions following [Hat07].

Let NN be a 33-manifold. A surface Σ\Sigma in NN is incompressible if every loop in Σ\Sigma bounding a disk in NN bounds a disk in Σ\Sigma, too. We write N|ΣN|\Sigma for a 33-manifold (with boundary) obtained from NN by removing Σ\Sigma together with some tubular neighborhood. Assume that NN is irreducible (see Section 2E). Then NN has a collection Σ\Sigma of incompressible tori such that each component of N|ΣN|\Sigma is either a Seifert fiber space or has no incompressible tori. A minimal such Σ\Sigma (in the sense of inclusion) is unique up to an isotopy [Hat07, Theorem 1.9], and N|ΣN|\Sigma is called a JSJ-decomposition of NN.

We now recall the notation for Seifert fibered spaces following [Hat07, §2.1]. Let BB be a compact surface of genus gg with rr boundary components, and let M0⟶B0M_{0}\longrightarrow B_{0} be an 𝕊1\mathbb{S}^{1}-bundle, where B0B_{0} is BB with kk disks D1,…,DkD_{1},\dots,D_{k} removed. The preimage Ti⊆M0T_{i}\subseteq M_{0} of ∂Di\partial D_{i} is a torus: we attach to it a solid torus 𝔻2×𝕊1\mathbb{D}^{2}\times\mathbb{S}^{1} in such a way that a meridian 0×𝕊10\times\mathbb{S}^{1} is attached to a loop in TiT_{i} whose preimage in its universal cover is a line of slope piqi\tfrac{p_{i}}{q_{i}}. The resulting manifold is a Seifert fibered space M⁡(g,r,p1q1,…,pkqk)M(g,r;\tfrac{p_{1}}{q_{1}},\dots,\tfrac{p_{k}}{q_{k}}). It is a graph manifold. Its graph has one vertex corresponding to M0M_{0} and kk maximal twigs, whose type is a continued fraction expansion of piqi\tfrac{p_{i}}{q_{i}}. This graph is normal whenever a Seifert fibration is unique, see [Neu81, 5.7]. Few important exceptions, including lens spaces 𝕊3/ℤp\mathbb{S}^{3}/\mathbb{Z}_{p}, are listed in [Hat07, Theorem 2.3]. Their normal graphs are described in [Neu81, 6.1].

Let again M=∂Tub⁡(D)M=\partial\mathrm{Tub}(D) be as in Notation 4.2. The following result can be inferred from the computation of Γ⁡(M)\Gamma(M) in Figure 4 using the algorithm in [Neu81, §5]. Nonetheless, we sketch a direct argument using the geometric description of incompressible tori in MM deduced in [BW01, Lemma 2.2] from [HT85].

Proposition 4.7 (JSJ decomposition of MM).

Let Σ1,Σ2⊆M\Sigma_{1},\Sigma_{2}\subseteq M be the plumbing tori at L1,0∩L2,0L_{1,0}\cap L_{2,0} and L1,0∩L2,∞L_{1,0}\cap L_{2,\infty}, see Section 2E. Then the JSJ decomposition of MM is

  1. (a)

    M|(Σ1⊔Σ2)=M⁡(2,0,1d1)⊔M⁡(2,0,1d2)M|(\Sigma_{1}\sqcup\Sigma_{2})=M(2,0;\tfrac{1}{d_{1}})\sqcup M(2,0;\tfrac{1}{d_{2}}) if d1,d2≠1d_{1},d_{2}\neq 1,

  2. (b)

    M|Σ1=M⁡(2,0,1d2)M|\Sigma_{1}=M(2,0;\tfrac{1}{d_{2}}) if d1=1d_{1}=1 and d2>1d_{2}>1,

  3. (c)

    M=M⁡(0,0,12,13,16)M=M(0,0;\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{3},\tfrac{1}{6}) if d1=d2=1d_{1}=d_{2}=1.

Let γj,δj\gamma_{j},\delta_{j} be as in Proposition 4.5. Then δj\delta_{j} is the singular fiber of M⁡(2,0,1dj)M(2,0;\tfrac{1}{d_{j}}) and γj\gamma_{j} is a general one.

By Theorem 1.4, MM is a 00-surgery on 𝕊3\mathbb{S}^{3} along K=K[2​d1,2​d2]K=K_{[2d_{1},2d_{2}]}. Because K[2,2]K_{[2,2]} is just a trefoil, (c) follows from [Mos71, Proposition 3.1] which completely describes surgeries on torus knots. Assume d2>1d_{2}>1. If d1>1d_{1}>1, too, then cutting along Σ1⊔Σ2\Sigma_{1}\sqcup\Sigma_{2} in case (a) corresponds to removing the edges of the circular subgraph in Figure 4(b), and decorating the leftmost vertices with r=2r=2, i.e. puncturing the base spheres twice. If d1=1d_{1}=1 then cutting along Σ1\Sigma_{1} corresponds to removing the loop in Figure 4(c) and adding boundary as before. This shows the equalities in (a)–(b), and proves that MM and, if d1=1d_{1}=1, M|ΣiM|\Sigma_{i} for i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\} are not Seifert fibered: indeed, Γ⁡(M|Σi)\Gamma(M|\Sigma_{i}) is not one of the graphs in [Neu81, 5.7, 6.1]. It remains to show that Σ1,Σ2⊆M\Sigma_{1},\Sigma_{2}\subseteq M are incompressible.

The 33-manifold MM is irreducible by [HT85, Theorem 2] (it also follows from Lemma 2.9(b)). Put M0=𝕊3∖Tub⁡(K)⊆MM_{0}=\mathbb{S}^{3}\setminus\mathrm{Tub}(K)\subseteq M. Put M0=𝕊3∖Tub⁡(K)⊆MM_{0}=\mathbb{S}^{3}\setminus\mathrm{Tub}(K)\subseteq M. By [HT85, Proposition 1(1) and the proof of Proposition 2] there are, up to isotopy, at most two incompressible surfaces Σ0⊆M0\Sigma_{0}\subseteq M_{0} such that the surfaces Σ⊆M\Sigma\subseteq M obtained by capping Σ0\Sigma_{0} are tori (see also proof of [BW01, Lemma 2.2]). Such Σ0\Sigma_{0} are denoted by S1​(0)S_{1}(0) and S1​(1)S_{1}(1) in [HT85], and they have exactly one boundary component each. By [Prz83, Proposition 1.5(a)] they are unknotted (see Definition 1.3 loc. cit), so by Theorem 1.4 loc. cit, Σ\Sigma remains incompressible. Moreover, by [HT85, Theorem 1(e)] S1​(0)S_{1}(0) is isotopic to S1​(1)S_{1}(1) if and only if d1=1d_{1}=1. Thus our claim will follow once we show that Σ=Σ1,Σ2\Sigma=\Sigma_{1},\Sigma_{2} for Σ0=S1​(0),S1​(1)\Sigma_{0}=S_{1}(0),S_{1}(1).

To this end, we recall the description of S1​(0)S_{1}(0), S0​(1)S_{0}(1) from [HT85, p. 227, Fig. 1]. Consider Figure 2 as a knot in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}, and let p{p} be a vertical plane between the “twists”. It meets the knot in four points. Hence S1​(0)S_{1}(0) caps to Σ1\Sigma_{1}. To see the 11-handles of S1​(1)S_{1}(1), we need to change the base point from q{q} to its complement. Remark 4.8 (A direct argument for minimality of Σ\Sigma).

In the above proof, we have used the classification of graph manifolds to show that the collections Σ1⊔Σ2\Sigma_{1}\sqcup\Sigma_{2} in (a) and Σ1\Sigma_{1} in (b) of incompressible tori decomposing MM to Seifert fibered spaces is minimal. However, this can be also seen directly, as follows.

First, we note that since Γ⁡(M|Σi)\Gamma(M|\Sigma_{i}) is a tree, one can use van Kampen theorem as in [Mum61] to compute

(4.2) π1(M|Σ1)=⟨δ1,δ2|[γ1,γ2]=1⟩, where δj and γj=δjdj are as in Remark 4.6.\pi_{1}(M|\Sigma_{1})=\langle\delta_{1},\delta_{2}|[\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2}]=1\rangle,\mbox{ where }\delta_{j}\mbox{ and }\gamma_{j}=\delta_{j}^{d_{j}}\mbox{ are as in Remark \ref{rem:pi_1-Mumford}.}

Suppose that d1,d2>1d_{1},d_{2}>1, but M|ΣiM|\Sigma_{i} is Seifert fibered for some i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\}. Then by [Hat07, Proposition 1.11], the incompressible torus Σ3−i⊆M|Σi\Sigma_{3-i}\subseteq M|\Sigma_{i} is either horizontal or vertical. In the first case, it covers the base orbifold, which has two boundary components, so comparing Euler characteristics as done in [Hat07, p. 22] shows that M|ΣiM|\Sigma_{i} has no singular fibers, so M|Σi≅(𝔻1×𝕊1)×𝕊1M|\Sigma_{i}\cong(\mathbb{D}^{1}\times\mathbb{S}^{1})\times\mathbb{S}^{1}, a contradiction with (4.2). In the second case, cutting M|ΣiM|\Sigma_{i} further along Σ3−i\Sigma_{3-i} preserves the Seifert fibration: therefore by the equality in (a), it restricts to the unique one on M⁡(2,0,1dj)M(2,0;\tfrac{1}{d_{j}}). Hence after gluing Σ3−i\Sigma_{3-i} back, the fiber of one fibration becomes a loop around the degenerate fiber of the other. This is a contradiction, because the former is central in π1\pi_{1}, and the latter is not.

Suppose now that d2>1d_{2}>1, but MM is Seifert fibered. Again, the incompressible torus Σ1\Sigma_{1} is either horizontal or vertical. In the first case, since M|Σ1M|\Sigma_{1} is connected, [Hat07, p. 22] implies that M|Σ1≅Σ1×𝔻1M|\Sigma_{1}\cong\Sigma_{1}\times\mathbb{D}^{1}, a contradiction with (4.2). In the second case, we obtain that M|Σ1M|\Sigma_{1} is a Seifert fiber space. We have shown that this is possible only if d1=1d_{1}=1, in which case the general fiber is represented by γ1∈π1​(M)\gamma_{1}\in\pi_{1}(M). In particular, ⟨γ1⟩⊆π1​(M)\langle\gamma_{1}\rangle\subseteq\pi_{1}(M) is a (nontrivial) central subgroup. Hence by (4.1) δ2=[γ1,λ]=1\delta_{2}=[\gamma_{1},\lambda]=1 and δ1=[δ2d2,λ−1]=1\delta_{1}=[\delta_{2}^{d_{2}},\lambda^{-1}]=1, so γ1=1\gamma_{1}=1; a contradiction.

5. ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-fibrations and complete algebraic vector fields on Sp1,p2S_{p_{1},p_{2}}

In this section we prove Theorem 1.6(b). It follows from [KKL20, Theorem 1.6] that a flow of any complete algebraic vector field on Sp1,p2S_{p_{1},p_{2}} preserves some ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-fibration of Sp1,p2S_{p_{1},p_{2}} (see Proposition 5.5(c) for details). Therefore, to understand AAuthol​(Sp1,p2)\mathrm{AAut}_{\mathrm{hol}}(S_{p_{1},p_{2}}) we need to classify all ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-fibrations of Sp1,p2S_{p_{1},p_{2}}.

Their degenerate fibers are affine curves with Euler characteristic at least etop​(ℂ∗)e_{\mathrm{top}}(\mathbb{C}^{*}), see [Miy01, III.1.8], i.e. unions of ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*} and ℂ1\mathbb{C}^{1}. Therefore, we begin by classifying all curves in Sp1,p2S_{p_{1},p_{2}} which are isomorphic to ℂ1\mathbb{C}^{1}. This is done in Lemma 5.2. In Lemma 5.3 we show that any ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-fibration of Sp1,p2S_{p_{1},p_{2}} comes from a ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-fibration of a complement of suitably chosen pair of disjoint ℂ1\mathbb{C}^{1}’s; which by Lemma 5.4 turns out to be a torus ℂ∗×ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}\times\mathbb{C}^{*}. The union of such tori is exactly the complement of ZZ from Theorem 1.6(b).

Lemma 5.3.

For any ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-fibration of SS one can find on SS two disjoint, vertical curves isomorphic to ℂ1\mathbb{C}^{1}, whose closures Γ1,Γ2⊆X\Gamma_{1},\Gamma_{2}\subseteq X satisfy Γi2⩾−1\Gamma_{i}^{2}\geqslant-1, with strict inequality if Γi⋅D⩾2\Gamma_{i}\cdot D\geqslant 2.

In the following, we fix coordinates on S=Sp1,p2S=S_{p_{1},p_{2}}, treating it as a closed subset of ℂ4\mathbb{C}^{4} given by (5.1).

Lemma 5.4 (Open tori in SS).

    σ⁡(xj)=vj,σ⁡(x3−j)=(vj−1)​v3−j−1,σ⁡(yj)=(vj−1−p^j​(vj)​v3−j)⋅(vjdj​v3−j)−1,σ⁡(y3−j)=v3−j;\sigma(x_{j})=v_{j},\quad\sigma(x_{3-j})=(v_{j}-1)v_{3-j}^{-1},\quad\sigma(y_{j})=(v_{j}-1-\widehat{p}_{j}(v_{j})v_{3-j})\cdot(v_{j}^{d_{j}}v_{3-j})^{-1},\quad\sigma(y_{3-j})=v_{3-j};
  3. (c)

    In case p1=p2=1p_{1}=p_{2}=1: U=S∖(C+Lj,1)U=S\setminus(C+L_{j,1}) for some j∈{1,2}j\in\{1,2\} and

    σ(xj)=−(v2+1)v1−1,σ(x3−j)=−(v1+v2+1)⋅(v1v2)−1,σ(yj)=(v1+1)v2−1,σ(y3−j)=v2.\sigma(x_{j})=-(v_{2}+1)v_{1}^{-1},\quad\sigma(x_{3-j})=-(v_{1}+v_{2}+1)\cdot(v_{1}v_{2})^{-1},\quad\sigma(y_{j})=(v_{1}+1)v_{2}^{-1},\quad\sigma(y_{3-j})=v_{2}.

The volume form d​v1v1∧d​v2v2\tfrac{dv_{1}}{v_{1}}\wedge\tfrac{dv_{2}}{v_{2}} on UU extends, up to a sign, to a volume form d​x1x1∧d​x2x2\tfrac{dx_{1}}{x_{1}}\wedge\tfrac{dx_{2}}{x_{2}}.

We check that by a direct computation that σ\sigma is zero on the ideal of SS, so it gives a morphism ℂ∗×ℂ∗⟶S\mathbb{C}^{*}\times\mathbb{C}^{*}\longrightarrow S. It has a rational inverse, given by

(a) vj↦xj,j∈{1,2};(b) vj↦xj,v3−j↦y3−j;(c) v1↦y1y2−1,v2↦y3−j.\mbox{\ref{item:AA} }v_{j}\mapsto x_{j},\ j\in\{1,2\};\quad\mbox{\ref{item:AL} }v_{j}\mapsto x_{j},v_{3-j}\mapsto y_{3-j};\quad\mbox{\ref{item:LC} }v_{1}\mapsto y_{1}y_{2}-1,v_{2}\mapsto y_{3-j}.

This inverse is regular on the complement of:

(a) {x1x2=0}=(A1+A2)|S;(b) {xjy3−j=0}=(Aj+Lj,1)|S;(c) {y3−j(1−y1y2)=0}=(Lj,1+C)|S;\mbox{\ref{item:AA} }\{x_{1}x_{2}=0\}=(A_{1}+A_{2})|_{S};\quad\mbox{\ref{item:AL} }\{x_{j}y_{3-j}=0\}=(A_{j}+L_{j,1})|_{S};\quad\mbox{\ref{item:LC} }\{y_{3-j}(1-y_{1}y_{2})=0\}=(L_{j,1}+C)|_{S};

and sends d​v1v1∧d​v2v2\tfrac{dv_{1}}{v_{1}}\wedge\tfrac{dv_{2}}{v_{2}} to ±d​x1x1∧d​x2x2\pm\tfrac{dx_{1}}{x_{1}}\wedge\tfrac{dx_{2}}{x_{2}}. This proves the lemma. ∎

The formulas {y3−j=0}=Lj,1|S\{y_{3-j}=0\}=L_{j,1}|_{S}, {y1y2=1}=C|S\{y_{1}y_{2}=1\}=C|_{S} used in the above proof do not hold for general p1,p2p_{1},p_{2}, but they do hold under the assumptions of (b) and (c), respectively.

Proposition 5.5 (Complete algebraic vector fields on Sp1,p2S_{p_{1},p_{2}}, cf. [KK11, Theorem 19]).
  1. (a)

    Every ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-fibration of SS restricts to a ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-fibration of one of the open tori U⊆SU\subseteq S from Lemma 5.4

  2. (b)

    For any U⊆SU\subseteq S from Lemma 5.4 and any aj⩾dja_{j}\geqslant d_{j}, j∈{1,2}j\in\{1,2\}, the complete vector field νa1,a2=v1a1​v2a2​(a2​v1​∂∂v1−a1​v2​∂∂v2)\nu_{a_{1},a_{2}}=v_{1}^{a_{1}}v_{2}^{a_{2}}(a_{2}v_{1}\tfrac{\partial}{\partial v_{1}}-a_{1}v_{2}\tfrac{\partial}{\partial v_{2}}) on UU extends to a complete vector field on SS.

  3. (c)

    Every complete algebraic vector field on SS restricts to a complete vector field on some torus U⊆SU\subseteq S from Lemma 5.4. In particular, it has divergence zero with respect to the volume form d​x1x1∧d​x2x2\tfrac{dx_{1}}{x_{1}}\wedge\tfrac{dx_{2}}{x_{2}}.

  4. (d)

    For each open torus U⊆SU\subseteq S from Lemma 5.4, the group AAuthol​(S)∩AAuthol​(U)\mathrm{AAut}_{\mathrm{hol}}(S)\cap\mathrm{AAut}_{\mathrm{hol}}(U) acts on UU mm-transitively for every mm.

(a) Fix a ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-fibration pp of SS and let Γ1,Γ2⊆X\Gamma_{1},\Gamma_{2}\subseteq X be as in Lemma 5.3. Then pp restricts to a ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-fibration of U=S∖(Γ1+Γ2)U=S\setminus(\Gamma_{1}+\Gamma_{2}). We claim that UU is as in Lemma 5.4. Because for i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\} Γi∩S≅ℂ1\Gamma_{i}\cap S\cong\mathbb{C}^{1}, Γi\Gamma_{i} is one of the curves from Lemma 5.2. If {Γ1,Γ2}={A1,A2}\{\Gamma_{1},\Gamma_{2}\}=\{A_{1},A_{2}\} then UU is as in Lemma 5.4(a). Assume that Γ1=C\Gamma_{1}=C. Because C⋅D=2C\cdot D=2, by Lemma 5.3 0⩽Γ12=2−d1−d20\leqslant\Gamma_{1}^{2}=2-d_{1}-d_{2}, so d1=d2=1d_{1}=d_{2}=1, i.e. p1=p2=1p_{1}=p_{2}=1. In this case, C∩SC\cap S meets Aj∩SA_{j}\cap S for both j∈{1,2}j\in\{1,2\}, so Γ2=L1,j\Gamma_{2}=L_{1,j} for some j∈{1,2}j\in\{1,2\} and therefore UU is as in Lemma 5.4(c). We are left with the case when Γ1=L1,j\Gamma_{1}=L_{1,j} for some j∈{1,2}j\in\{1,2\} and Γ2≠C\Gamma_{2}\neq C. As before, the condition Γ12⩾−1\Gamma_{1}^{2}\geqslant-1 from Lemma 5.3 implies by Lemma 5.2(b) that dj=1d_{j}=1, i. e. pj=1p_{j}=1. In this case, L1,j∩SL_{1,j}\cap S meets A3−j∩SA_{3-j}\cap S and L3−j,1∩SL_{3-j,1}\cap S, so Γ2=Aj\Gamma_{2}=A_{j} or CC. The second case is excluded by assumption, so the first case holds and UU is as in Lemma 5.4(b).

(b) follows from a direct computation, see [And00, Corollary 2].

(c) Part (b) implies that complete algebraic vector fields on SS do not share a rational first integral. Hence by [KKL20, Theorem 1.6], for any complete algebraic vector field ξ\xi on SS there is a ℂ1\mathbb{C}^{1}- or ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-fibration of SS preserved by the flow of ξ\xi. Because κ⁡(S)=0\kappa(S)=0, SS admits no ℂ1\mathbb{C}^{1}-fibrations, hence ξ\xi preserves one of the ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-fibrations from (a). In each case, the complement of UU is a union of vertical curves isomorphic to ℂ1\mathbb{C}^{1}, so the flow of ξ\xi cannot send them to non-degenerate fibers in UU. It follows that ξ\xi restricts to a complete vector field on UU. In particular, by [And00, Corollary 1] it preserves the volume form d​v1v1∧d​v2v2\tfrac{dv_{1}}{v_{1}}\wedge\tfrac{dv_{2}}{v_{2}}, where v1,v2v_{1},v_{2} are coordinates on U≅ℂ∗×ℂ∗U\cong\mathbb{C}^{*}\times\mathbb{C}^{*}. Lemma 5.4 implies that ξ\xi preserves d​x1x1∧d​x2x2\tfrac{dx_{1}}{x_{1}}\wedge\tfrac{dx_{2}}{x_{2}}, too.

(d) Choose integers ai​ja_{ij}, i,j∈{1,2}i,j\in\{1,2\} such that ai​j⩾dja_{ij}\geqslant d_{j} and det[ai​j]=1\det[a_{ij}]=1, and put σi=νai​1,ai​2\sigma_{i}=\nu_{a_{i1},a_{i2}}, fi=v1ai​1​v2ai​2∈ker⁡σi∖ker⁡σ3−if_{i}=v_{1}^{a_{i1}}v_{2}^{a_{i2}}\in\ker\sigma_{i}\setminus\ker\sigma_{3-i}. Now the result follows from [KK11, Propostion 8.9]. Indeed, although that result is formulated in loc. cit. for G=AAuthol​(U)G=\mathrm{AAut}_{\mathrm{hol}}(U), the proof actually shows mm-transitivity for the group generated by the elements of the flows of q⁡(fi)⋅σiq(f_{i})\cdot\sigma_{i} for q∈ℂ⁡[t]q\in\mathbb{C}[t]. ∎

Part (a) was shown in Corollary 2.6(c). For (b), note that the open subset S∖ZS\setminus Z of SS is precisely the union of all U⊆SU\subseteq S from Lemma 5.4. By Proposition 5.5(c), S∖ZS\setminus Z is fixed by AAuthol​(S)\mathrm{AAut}_{\mathrm{hol}}(S). On the other hand, by Proposition 5.5(d) each U⊆SU\subseteq S from Lemma 5.4 is contained in a single orbit of AAuthol​(S)\mathrm{AAut}_{\mathrm{hol}}(S). Because every two such UU, being open and dense in SS, have nonempty intersection, they are all contained in the same orbit of AAuthol​(S)\mathrm{AAut}_{\mathrm{hol}}(S), which therefore equals S∖ZS\setminus Z. Proposition 5.5(d) implies that AAuthol​(S)\mathrm{AAut}_{\mathrm{hol}}(S) acts on this orbit mm-transitively for every mm, as claimed. ∎

Remark 5.6 (Density property for Sp1,p2S_{p_{1},p_{2}}).

In view of Theorem 1.6(b), it is natural to ask for an even stronger property than mm-transitivity of AAuthol​(S)\mathrm{AAut}_{\mathrm{hol}}(S), namely for the algebraic density property (ADP), see [KK11]. Recall that a smooth affine variety XX has ADP if the Lie algebra VFalg⁡(X)\operatorname{VF_{alg}}(X) of algebraic vector fields on XX coincides with the Lie algebra Liealg⁡(X)\operatorname{Lie_{alg}}(X) generated by complete ones. Since in our case all vector fields preserve ZZ, one should rather ask if the relative ADP holds, see [KLL15], namely, if there exists l⩾0l\geqslant 0 such that Il​VFalg⁡(S)⊆Liealg⁡(S)I^{l}\operatorname{VF_{alg}}(S)\subseteq\operatorname{Lie_{alg}}(S), where II is the ideal of ZZ. This, however, is not true since by Lemma 5.4(c) all elements of Liealg⁡(S)\operatorname{Lie_{alg}}(S) preserve the volume form ω=d​x1x1∧d​x2x2\omega=\tfrac{dx_{1}}{x_{1}}\wedge\tfrac{dx_{2}}{x_{2}}. Nonetheless, one could ask for the relative volume density property, defined as follows (see [KK16]). Let XX be a normal variety with a volume form ω\omega, and let Y⊆XY\subseteq X be a closed subset containing Sing⁡X\operatorname{Sing}X. Denote by VFalgω⁡(X,Y)\operatorname{VF_{alg}^{\omega}}(X,Y) the Lie algebra of those algebraic vector fields on XX which vanish on YY and preserve the volume form ω\omega; and by Liealgω⁡(X,Y)\operatorname{Lie_{alg}^{\omega}}(X,Y) the Lie algebra generated by complete vector fields in VFalgω⁡(X,Y)\operatorname{VF_{alg}^{\omega}}(X,Y). We say that XX has an algebraic volume density property (AVDP) relative to YY if there exists l⩾0l\geqslant 0 such that Il​VFalgω⁡(X,Y)⊆Liealgω⁡(X,Y)I^{l}\operatorname{VF_{alg}^{\omega}}(X,Y)\subseteq\operatorname{Lie_{alg}^{\omega}}(X,Y), where II is the ideal of YY. In this setting, one could ask the following:

Question.

Let Z⊆Sp1,p2Z\subseteq S_{p_{1},p_{2}} be as in Theorem 1.6(b). Does Sp1,p2S_{p_{1},p_{2}} have AVDP relative to ZZ?

For p1=p2=1p_{1}=p_{2}=1 (so Z=∅Z=\emptyset), the answer to this question is positive [KK16, Theorem 6].

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
